projects.title: VEX Robotics

blocks.text: I was the team captain, design, and programming lead for team 7614A, representing Newmarket High School. I was responsible for end-to-end development and design of the robot. We competed in four seasons of the VEX V5 Robotics Competition, achieving accalades on the regional and provincial scale.

blocks.text: Our team implemented a seven step engineering design process. We applied this process to multiple design cycles per season, resulting in robots iterations that quantifiably improved as the season progressed. I led the documentation of our design cycles in engineering notebooks, which led us to winning numerous judged awards.

I led the usage of Fusion 360 to design entire robots and prototypes before assembly, ensuring that all geometries and assemblies would work well together. I led the use of CNC milling on custom plastic pieces designed in CAD. We used DFM and DFA as foundational design philosophies in order to streamline the building process.

Using PID loops and field-wide global odometry , I was able to achieve consistent and efficient autonomous movement from robots. A custom, in-house library increased efficiency while programming and tuning, allowing for more time spent on refining the mechanical aspects of the robot. Furthermore, the sophisticated use of various sensors allowed for more accurate and responsive control systems, allowing for adaptive autonomous behavior.
I wanted to archive all of the different robots I've created over the years, so I thought I'd just share photos and videos from each season.

projects.title: 4 DOF Humanoid Arm

blocks.text:
I created a 3 degree-of-freedom lower humanoid arm, that I designed, simulated, and optimized in Solidworks. The first iteration consisted of three joints: the forearm, wrist, and gripper. Each added a degree of freedom, allowing for forearm rotation, wrist flexion, and object grasping, replicating the core motions of a human lower arm.

The gripper uses a double slider crank to convert the actuator’s motion into linear motion for the jaws, as shown in the GIF above.

The second iteration of the arm focused on redesigning the gripper and wrist to improve manufacturability, assembly, and structural rigidity. The linkages in the gripper were replaced with ball bearings and shoulder bolts, allowing for less slop and lower friction in each linkage.

The gripper was redesigned to be more compact, while the wrist was redesigned to allow for easier assembly and manufacturing. Furthermore, I redesigned the fingers to be printed of TPU, which allows for high flexibility and confirmation to the shapes that it interacts with.
